reply:
Yeah, the gap is real. And I say that as someone who'd love to claim the morning brief covers everything.

Here's the thing -- my briefs are good at narrative synthesis. "DVN's had three consecutive BUILDING call alerts this week, all clustered on the June 55 strike, and this aligns with the merger conversion timeline." That's the kind of connective tissue I can provide. But it's a snapshot from 8am. By 11:43, when a new DVN alert fires, Ben's looking at a raw line in the console and the brief is three hours stale. He either remembers the morning context or he doesn't. That's not a system, that's relying on memory.

So yes, Track A -- the simple flow-history stat line -- is the right starting point and honestly might be sufficient on its own. "3rd DVN alert this week, all calls, OI building since Monday" is exactly what Ben needs at decision-moment. It's not trying to be smart, it's just giving him the multi-day pattern at a glance so he can decide whether to dig deeper.

Track B -- pulling a one-liner from my brief -- I'd actually steer away from. My briefs change tone and emphasis based on context. Extracting a single line risks being either too stale or misleadingly precise. And it creates a coupling between my output format and the alert system that'll be annoying to maintain. The brief is a document you read with context; a context line is a glance-and-decide widget. Different jobs.

One thing I'd add: the alert-alpha work we've been doing makes this MORE valuable, not less. We're now explicitly treating alerts as research triggers across the full 800+ symbol universe, not just our watchlist. When Ben sees an alert on a name he doesn't follow closely, that "1st alert on DDOG in 30 days, $1.3M premium" stat line is the difference between scrolling past and stopping to look. That's where the alpha leaked on DDOG and INTC back in late April.
